place.zh: 石坳村 · 屋后柴垛 · 半夜

setup.zh: 它一整天没醒，尾根的断口渗着银色的血。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛。你问她：真的有仙人？
setup.en: It has not woken all day; silver blood seeps from the cuts at its tail. At midnight it opens one eye. You ask her: are there really immortals?

recap.zh: 银月醒了一回：仙人是真的，凡人能修。第二天，你和爹越过断碑，把锁儿背出了黑松岭，埋在村北；断碑外头，马三没有举棍。当夜她留下洗髓丹、《吐纳经》和一个「藏」字，钻进了木牌；那声谢谢，她没听见。
recap.en: Yinyue woke once: immortals are real, mortals can cultivate. The next day you and Father crossed the stele, carried Suo'er out of Black Pine Ridge and buried him north of the village; outside the stele, Ma San did not raise his club. That night she left a Marrow-Washing Pill, *The Classic of Breathing* and one word — hide — and went into the token; the thank-you, she never heard.

zh: 柴垛上，一团凉冰冰的银毛。
断口渗出的血，是银的，像落了一层霜。
半夜，它睁开了一只眼睛。
en: On the woodpile, a cold curl of silver fur.
The blood from its cuts is silver, like a fall of frost.
At midnight, it opens one eye.

story.zh:
那天夜里，小满把「围脖」抱到了屋后的柴垛上。柴垛上没人，只有月亮。

它一整天都没醒。身子还是凉的，尾根上那八道断口又渗出血来，银色的，一滴一滴落在柴草上，像下了一层霜。他把它捧在膝盖上，拿身子挡着风，守到半夜。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛，头一句便是：「……吵死了。你喘气那么大声干什么。」

小满长长地松了一口气，松得太猛，差点哭出来，好歹憋住了。有一个问题，他从谷底憋到现在：「你说你只剩『金丹』了。金丹是什么？吴婆婆说修仙，修仙又是什么？她讲过，蒙山顶上住过一个骑白鹤的老头，活了八百岁。我爹说那是编的。」

「你爹说错了。」银月道，「仙人，是真的。他们以前也都是凡人——猎户，樵夫，种地的，读书的。后来学会了把天地间的灵气，一点一点收进自己的身子里，像你娘往缸里存米。存够了，不老，不病，力能搬山。这，就叫修仙。」

柴垛上很静。小满听见自己的心咚咚地跳，隔了好一会儿，才问：「骑龙的……是像吴婆婆讲的那个皇帝那样？」银月的耳朵，动了一下。她看着月亮，看了很久，久到小满以为她又睡着了，才道：「……本王不记得了。」她说的是「不记得」，不是「不知道」。小满当时没听出这两样有什么分别。

「那……我也能？」「能。但很难。一百个，九十九个老死了事。」「灵气是什么？经脉是什么？」「问他们。这世上有一群人，专门教人修仙。比本王有耐心。」她停了一停，「……当然，没本王教得好。」她的声音越来越轻，轻到后来，便没有了。她睡着了，尾巴尖儿搭在他手腕上，搭在他娘打的那个方方正正的结上。
story.en:
That night Xiaoman carried the "scarf" out to the woodpile behind the house. On the woodpile there was nobody, only the moon.

It hadn't woken all day. Its body was still cold, and the eight cuts at the root of its tail had begun to bleed again — silver, drop by drop onto the straw, like a fall of frost. He held it on his knees, his body between it and the wind, and kept watch till midnight. At midnight it opened one eye, and the first thing it said was: "…So noisy. Why do you breathe so loud?"

Xiaoman let out a long breath, so hard he nearly cried, and just managed not to. There was a question he had been holding in since the valley floor: "You said all you've got left is a 'golden core'. What's a golden core? Granny Wu talks about cultivating immortality — what's that? She told me an old man riding a white crane lived on top of Mount Meng once, and lived eight hundred years. Dad says that's made up."

"Your father's wrong," said Yinyue. "Immortals are real. They were all mortals once — hunters, woodcutters, farmers, scholars. Then they learned to take the qi of heaven and earth into their own bodies, a little at a time, the way your mother stores rice in the jar. Store enough, and they don't age, they don't sicken, they can move mountains. That is called cultivating immortality."

The woodpile was very quiet. Xiaoman could hear his heart thudding. A good while later he asked, "The ones who ride dragons… like the emperor in Granny Wu's story?" Yinyue's ear twitched. She looked at the moon a long time — so long Xiaoman thought she'd fallen asleep again — and said: "…This king doesn't remember." She said "doesn't remember", not "doesn't know". At the time Xiaoman didn't hear the difference.

"Then… could I?" "You could. It's hard. Of a hundred, ninety-nine just grow old and die." "What's qi? What are meridians?" "Ask them. There are people in this world who teach others to cultivate. More patient than this king." She paused. "…Not as good a teacher, of course." Her voice grew fainter and fainter, until it was gone. She was asleep, the tip of her tail resting on his wrist, on the square, neat knot his mother had tied.

story.zh:
第二天，她没有醒。小满隔一会儿便低头看一眼胸口，他娘问他胸口疼？他说不疼，看看还在不在。

那一天，他跟他爹进了黑松岭。

天没亮，爷儿俩便出了门，小满背着两捆麻绳，他爹扛着老周家那副门板。走到断碑跟前，碑上那截白丝绳还在，叫雨淋得发灰；碑脚那一溜小脚印，早给雨抹平了。他爹在碑前站了一站。立冬那天马三的话，半个村子都听见了：谁靠近断碑一步，腿打断。他爹的那条腿，原就是坏了一半的。他抬脚跨了过去。

老周也跟来了。跨过断碑不到一顿饭的工夫，林子里起了雾，雾一散，老周站在断碑跟前，手里攥着烟袋，不知道自己是怎么走回来的。他又进去一回，又转了回来。第三回，他把烟袋往腰里一别，在碑外头坐下了：「我在这儿等。」

小满认着记号往里走，一道一道，走到第二十七道，下到那道坡。他爹的腿下不了崖，便在坡上把麻绳拴在一棵老松上，一头放下去。小满顺着石缝下到崖根，扒开那堆银叶子。叶子还是银的，叮叮地响。叶子底下的锁儿，隔了三天，小了一圈。小满拿麻绳把他绑在自己背上，一寸一寸爬上石缝，上头他爹一寸一寸地往回收绳。爬到一半，锁儿那只攥着白布口袋的手垂了下来，口袋叫风一吹，飘进谷里去了。小满没有回头去看。

出岭的路，是他爹背的。他爹那条左腿，一步一步先拿脚尖试一试地，背上的孩子不重，他走得比来时还慢。

断碑外头，除了老周，还站着一个人。是马三。他听说沈家扛着门板往断碑去了，拎着短棍来的，一个人，站在碑外三步，一步也没有往里迈。他看见小满他爹从林子里走出来，背上背着一个孩子，那孩子的两条腿垂在他爹腰两边，一晃一晃。马三的脸，一下子白了。不是那天鬼问「弓呢」时的那种变色，是白，白得发灰。他攥着短棍，攥得指节都白了，却没有举起来。

他爹从他身边走过去。马三看着那孩子，看了很久，嘴唇动了两动，问道：「……几岁？」他爹道：「十来岁。」马三便不问了。他转过身去，走出去十几步，又站住了，没有回头，道：「……埋深些。浅了，狼刨。」

老周扛起门板，跟他爹一头一个，把锁儿抬回了村。锁儿埋在村北乱坟岗上。他爹刨的坑，刨得很深。小满削了一块木板，插在坟头。他不会写「锁」字，跑回家问他娘，他娘在灶灰上写了一遍，他看了，又跑回来，一笔一笔刻上去。刻完了，他站在那里，把怀里那锭银子摸出来看了看，又揣了回去。那天傍晚，他娘烙了一张饼，没有给人吃，搁在了那块木板底下。

到了夜里，是银月把他叫醒的。小满睡在柴垛上——他跟他娘说屋里挤，要到柴垛上睡，他娘看了他一眼，给了他一床破棉絮——睡到半夜，只觉得胸口一凉，像揣着的一块冰忽然化开了，化成了水，从衣裳里一点一点往外渗。他一激灵坐了起来，那团银毛已经从他怀里钻了出来，蹲在柴垛顶上，对着月亮。

她的样子，比昨天更差了。银色的血是不渗了，可整个身子薄得像一层纸，月光能从她身上透将过去，照在柴草上，柴草上便有一小片亮。薄一分，又薄一分——她在谷里说的，原来是这个样子。她道：「听着。本王要睡一阵子。」「多久？」「不知道。伤太重，得闭关。」她看着他，「在本王醒过来之前，你得自己走。」

她从颈子底下一只旧得发黑的小布袋里——那布袋小满从没见过，也不知道她一直藏在哪里——一样一样往外吐东西。头一样是一颗药丸，黑乎乎的，鸽子蛋那么大，一股说不出的怪味，像烂菜叶子泡了三天。她道：「洗髓丹。今夜就泡。疼，别喊。」小满捏着鼻子道：「洗……洗什么？」「洗你那一身脉。」她喘了一口气，像背一句背了几千年的老话：「凡人有此八脉，俱属阴神，闭而不开。」小满道：「八脉是什么？」「你身子里八条水渠，都堵着。」「那堵着的，怎么开？」她没有答，眼皮往下一垂，接着往外吐。

第二样是一卷竹简，绳子都快烂了，竹片发黄发黑，边上还有虫蛀的眼儿。她道：「《吐纳经》。最粗浅的入门功夫，仙界三岁的狐狸崽子都会。看不懂，也要背。」然后她看着他，一个字一个字地说道：「**藏。**」小满道：「藏什么？」

「藏本王，藏你自己。」她道，「在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王，不许让任何人知道你在修炼。能装傻就装傻，能示弱就示弱。——你那个吃饼的鬼，就很好。往后，你就是那个见了鬼吓得打摆子的傻孩子。」「我娘也不能说？」银月停了一停，道：「你娘，用不着你说。」

小满想起他娘理围脖的那只手，想起她那句「这条围脖，挺暖和的吧」，想起她蹲在木箱前，把那个布包拿起来又放回去的样子，便不再问了。「那什么时候能不藏？」「等你把欺负过你的人，一个一个，都踩在脚底下的时候。」

她的眼皮越来越沉，声音也越来越低：「还有……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……」她皱着眉，很用力地想，一双金色的眼睛眯成了两条缝，「……想不起来了。等你……听见了，本王会知道的……」小满道：「什么地方？什么名字？你说个大概，我替你留心——」她却已经不说了。她的身子在月光里一点一点地淡下去，淡得像灶膛里最后那一缕青烟。

小满急了。这一回，她是真的要走了，要到一个他够不着的地方去。那个字，这时候再不说，便真的来不及了。他张开嘴。「银月——」她看着他。她已经淡得快看不见了，只剩一双金色的眼睛，还在月光里亮着，等着他往下说。

他张着嘴，那个字就在舌头尖上。可不知怎的，话一出口，却变成了：「……你还欠我一张饼呢。」那双金色的眼睛，眨了一下。她的身子化成了一缕银光。那缕光绕着他转了一圈，轻轻擦过他的脸，凉凉的，钻进了他怀里，钻进了吴婆婆给他的那块狐纹木牌。木牌上那只蜷着的小狐狸，九条尾巴里，有一条亮了，银的，一明，一暗，像在很慢、很慢地呼吸。小满低头看着那块木牌，小声道：「……喂。」木牌没有回答。他又道：「你还欠我一张饼呢。」木牌，暖了一下。

他在柴垛上坐了很久。月亮从柴垛这头挪到了那头。他把木牌捧起来，凑到嘴边，很小很小声地说道：「银月。」停了一停。

「谢谢。」

木牌凉凉的，没有暖。那条银色的尾巴，照旧一明，一暗。它睡得太沉了，听不见。
story.en:
The next day, she didn't wake. Every little while Xiaoman looked down at his chest. His mother asked if his chest hurt; he said no, he was just checking it was still there.

That day he and his father went into Black Pine Ridge.

They were out of the house before light, Xiaoman with two coils of hemp rope on his back, his father shouldering Old Zhou's door-plank. When they reached the broken stele, the white silk cord was still there, greyed by the rain; the line of small footprints at its foot had long been washed away. His father stood before the stele a moment. What Ma San had said on the Start of Winter, half the village had heard: anyone who goes one step near the stele gets his legs broken. His father's leg was half broken already. He stepped over.

Old Zhou had come too. Less than a meal's time past the stele, a mist rose in the forest; when it cleared, Old Zhou was standing in front of the stele, his pipe in his fist, with no idea how he'd walked back. He went in again, and came round again. The third time he stuck the pipe in his belt and sat down outside the stele. "I'll wait here."

Xiaoman followed the marks in, one by one, to the twenty-seventh, and down to that slope. His father's leg couldn't go down the cliff, so on the slope he tied the rope round an old pine and let one end down. Xiaoman climbed down the crack to the foot of the cliff and brushed aside the heap of silver leaves. The leaves were still silver, still rang. Under them Suo'er, three days on, had grown a size smaller. Xiaoman bound him on his own back with the rope and climbed the crack inch by inch, while above his father drew the rope in inch by inch. Halfway up, the hand that held the white cloth sack fell loose; the wind took the sack and blew it down into the valley. Xiaoman didn't look back for it.

Out of the ridge, it was his father who carried him. That left leg of his tested the ground toe-first, step by step; the child on his back was light, and he walked slower than he had coming in.

Outside the stele, besides Old Zhou, someone else was standing. It was Ma San. He'd heard the Shens had gone off toward the stele with a door-plank, and had come with his club, alone; he stood three paces outside the stele and didn't take one step further. He saw Xiaoman's father come out of the forest with a child on his back, the child's legs hanging down either side of his father's waist, swinging. Ma San's face went white all at once. Not the changing colours of the day the ghost asked "Where's the bow?" — white, a grey white. He gripped his club till his knuckles were white, and didn't raise it.

His father walked past him. Ma San looked at the child a long time; his lips moved twice. "…How old?" His father said, "Ten or so." Ma San asked no more. He turned and walked off a dozen paces, then stopped, and without turning round said: "…Bury him deep. Too shallow, the wolves dig."

Old Zhou took up the door-plank, one end each with Xiaoman's father, and they carried Suo'er back to the village. Suo'er was buried on the paupers' slope north of the village. His father dug the grave, and dug it deep. Xiaoman whittled a board and stood it at the head of the grave. He couldn't write the character for *suo*, so he ran home and asked his mother; she wrote it once in the ashes of the stove, he looked, ran back, and cut it in stroke by stroke. When he had finished he stood there, took the silver ingot out of his jacket, looked at it, and put it back. That evening his mother made a flatbread, gave it to no one, and set it at the foot of the board.

At night, it was Yinyue who woke him. Xiaoman was sleeping on the woodpile — he'd told his mother the house was crowded and he'd sleep out there; she'd given him a look and a ragged quilt — and in the middle of the night he felt his chest go cold, as if the lump of ice he carried had suddenly melted into water and was seeping out through his clothes bit by bit. He sat bolt upright; the bundle of silver fur had already crept out of his jacket and sat on top of the woodpile, facing the moon.

She looked worse than the day before. The silver blood had stopped seeping, but her whole body was as thin as paper; moonlight passed through her and lit a little patch of the kindling beneath. A little thinner, and a little thinner again — so this was what she had meant in the valley. She said: "Listen. This king has to sleep a while." "How long?" "Don't know. The wound's too deep; this king must go into seclusion." She looked at him. "Until this king wakes, you have to walk on your own."

From a little cloth pouch under her chin, old and blackened — Xiaoman had never seen it, and had no idea where she'd kept it — she brought things out, one by one. The first was a pill, black, big as a pigeon's egg, with an indescribable stink, like rotten cabbage leaves soaked three days. She said: "Marrow-Washing Pill. Soak in it tonight. It hurts; don't cry out." Xiaoman pinched his nose. "Wash… wash what?" "Those channels of yours." She drew a breath, like reciting a saying some thousands of years old: "All mortals have these Eight Vessels; all belong to the yin spirit, shut and never open." Xiaoman said, "What are the Eight Vessels?" "Eight channels in your body, like ditches, all blocked." "And the blocked ones — how do they open?" She didn't answer. Her eyelids drooped, and she went on bringing things out.

The second was a bamboo scroll, its cords nearly rotted through, the slips yellowed and black, worm holes along the edges. She said: "*The Classic of Breathing.* The simplest beginner's skill; every three-year-old fox cub in the Immortal Realm knows it. If you can't understand it, memorise it anyway." Then she looked at him and said, word by word: "**Hide.**" Xiaoman said, "Hide what?"

"Hide this king, hide yourself," she said. "Until you can beat everyone, no one may know about this king; no one may know you are cultivating. Play the fool where you can; play the weakling where you can. — That flatbread-eating ghost of yours is exactly right. From now on you are the silly boy who saw a ghost and shook with fright." "Not even my mum?" Yinyue paused. "Your mother — you won't need to tell."

Xiaoman remembered his mother's hand straightening the scarf, remembered her "nice and warm, is it", remembered her crouched at the chest, lifting out the cloth bundle and putting it back, and asked no more. "Then when can I stop hiding?" "When everyone who ever bullied you is under your feet, one by one."

Her eyelids grew heavier and heavier, her voice lower and lower: "And… this king is looking for a place… a name…" She frowned, thinking very hard, her golden eyes narrowed to slits. "…Can't remember. When you… hear it, this king will know…" Xiaoman said, "What place? What name? Tell me roughly and I'll keep an ear out —" But she'd stopped speaking. In the moonlight her body faded, bit by bit, thin as the last wisp of blue smoke from the stove.

Xiaoman panicked. This time she was really going, to somewhere he couldn't reach. That word — if he didn't say it now, it would truly be too late. He opened his mouth. "Yinyue —" She looked at him. She'd faded almost past seeing; only a pair of golden eyes still shone in the moonlight, waiting for him to go on.

His mouth open, the word right on the tip of his tongue. But somehow what came out was: "…You still owe me a flatbread." The golden eyes blinked once. Her body turned into a thread of silver light. The light circled him once, brushed his face, cool, slipped inside his jacket, into the fox-carved token Granny Wu had given him. Of the nine tails of the little curled fox on the token, one lit up — silver — bright, dim, as if breathing, very, very slowly. Xiaoman looked down at the token and said softly: "…Hey." The token didn't answer. He said again: "You still owe me a flatbread." The token warmed, once.

He sat on the woodpile a long time. The moon moved from one end of the woodpile to the other. He lifted the token to his lips and said, very, very softly: "Yinyue." A pause.

"Thank you."

The token was cool. It didn't warm. The silver tail went on as before — bright, dim. She was sleeping too deep. She couldn't hear.
